bull_bear.body: Grand Vitara is manufactured by Toyota Kirloskar at cost (no profit markup) under exclusive contract, making it a de facto Maruti product for accounting and margin purposes; 45-50% hybrid uptake in Grand Vitara exceeds industry expectations and signals consumer readiness for premium electrification; Haryana plant decision reflects operational logic over corporate accounting — Maruti owns the factory despite Suzuki’s global ownership
bull_bear.title: Non-obvious takeaways

bull_bear.body:
- Scale and share: India's largest passenger vehicle manufacturer, with a retail market share of about 40% in FY 2025-26 and a leadership position across almost all product segments; six of the top ten best-selling cars in the industry were from Maruti Suzuki
- Parent technology access: the Company 'offers relevant products and technology that Indian customers need by leveraging the unique ability of Suzuki Motor Corporation to design feature-rich, safer, environment-friendly products with world class quality at an affordable price'
- Export franchise built on the parent's network: export volumes of 447,774 units in FY 2025-26 across over 120 markets; nearly 50% of all passenger vehicles exported from India; India's leading PV exporter for the fifth consecutive year
- Distribution reach, especially non-urban: 366 sales outlets added in FY 2025-26, over 2,900 outlets in non-urban markets, and 868 new sales and service touchpoints taking the total to 10,527 (Chairman's message)
- Service and aftermarket network as a switching-cost moat: 5,926 service touchpoints, 1,574 parts distribution sales outlets, more than 95,500 unique parts and accessories, and over 50,000 independent workshops connected through Parts Kart
- CNG leadership: CNG options in 14 of 18 PV models and nearly 70% market share in that segment, with CNG PV sales up 19.7% y-o-y
- Multi-powertrain portfolio (CNG, mild hybrid, strong hybrid, BEV) taking green vehicles to nearly 52% of total PV sales in FY 2025-26 from about 48% the previous year
- Safety differentiation: six airbags and Electronic Stability Control standard on nearly 100% of the portfolio - 'the only OEM in the country to offer such safety features as standard across a wide and diverse portfolio'
- Supplier ecosystem and localisation: nearly 450 Tier-1 and about 1,500 Tier-2 suppliers, with localisation described as a key pillar of long-term supply chain resilience
- Digitalisation of the purchase journey: 24 of 26 customer interaction points digitalised, and over 39% of customers sourcing finance through Maruti Suzuki Smart Finance
bull_bear.title: Bull — competitive strengths

bull_bear.body:
- Risks associated with the increased scale of operations — The Company aims to scale production to four million units annually by FY 2030-31, nearly double its current capacity. It took almost 40 years to reach two million units; the next two million is to be added in just 7-8 years, a pace nearly five times faster. This requires significantly more human capital, financial investment and technical know-how plus faster decision-making, and stakeholder partners - suppliers, dealers and transporters - must scale in tandem.
- Continuity of component supplies across a concentrated supplier base — With nearly 450 Tier-1 and about 1,500 Tier-2 suppliers, supply disruption remains a major business continuity risk. Export restrictions on certain critical materials during the year highlighted the vulnerability of globally concentrated supply chains, and geopolitical tensions, trade restrictions and logistics disruptions may continue to affect supply availability. Mitigation is localisation, alternate sources, diversified sourcing locations and the Vendor Comprehensive Excellence Programme.
- Dependence on specialised materials and critical components sourced from a limited number of countries — Increasing adoption of advanced automotive technologies raises dependence on specialised materials and critical components whose supply chains remain concentrated in a few countries; in an increasingly dynamic geopolitical environment, material-availability risk is likely to persist. In the near term, geopolitical tensions in West Asia may exert pressure on profitability through higher commodity prices.
- Cost competitiveness of emerging and advanced technologies in a price-sensitive market — Electrification, software-defined vehicles, advanced electronics and connectivity are transforming the industry, but several of these technologies are yet to reach the cost competitiveness needed for widespread adoption in a price-sensitive market such as India. As the BEV, SHEV and advanced-feature portfolio expands, holding cost competitiveness while preserving affordability is a key strategic priority, addressed through localisation, value engineering and supplier base expansion.
- Commodity price volatility — Sudden and significant increases in the prices of metals, energy and other commodities can adversely impact profitability and business performance, a risk reinforced by recent geopolitical developments. This risk materialised in FY 2025-26: operating margin moderated to 8.4% from 10.0%, driven by adverse commodity prices and supply-side pressures, with the Company choosing not to pass on the full cost increases. Mitigation includes consumption optimisation, alternate materials, material circularity, hedging, forward contracts and long-term commercial arrangements.
- Capacity and capability for future readiness - skills, leadership pipeline and cultural continuity at scale — Scaling operations amid rapid technological transformation increases demand for new skillsets both internally and across value chain partners; at the same time, sustaining the organisational values, culture of partnership and continuous-improvement spirit built over four decades becomes harder as scale and workforce expand.
- Cybersecurity, including cyber risk in the supply chain — Cyber threats are growing and the Company protects information assets through employee education on phishing and proactive monitoring. It has created a cybersecurity assessment framework based on global standards for suppliers, and over 400 Tier-1 supplier partners have been assessed so far, on the view that supply-chain cyber resilience is a business-continuity issue.
- Foreign exchange exposure on imports and exports — The Company is exposed to fluctuations in foreign exchange rates, mainly on the import of components, raw materials and services and on the export of vehicles and services. It runs a structured exchange risk management policy and uses hedge instruments judiciously depending on market conditions and the currency view. The MD&A separately records a sharp depreciation of the rupee against the US dollar towards the end of the year.

outlook.title: Growth verticals / optionality

outlook.body:
- Growth strategy for FY 2030-31: during FY 2025-26 the Company completed the amalgamation of Suzuki Motor Gujarat Private Limited to enhance organisational agility, strengthened its SUV portfolio and diversified powertrains, accelerated capacity expansion, and announced an additional greenfield manufacturing facility in Gujarat.
- Accelerate capacity expansion and build flexibility: all new production lines are being made flexible enough to change platforms and models as required, and all new manufacturing facilities are designed with multi-powertrain flexibility to respond to future shifts in technology and customer demand.
- Balanced multi-powertrain / multi-pathway approach - CNG, mild hybrids, strong hybrids and battery electric vehicles, extending to ICE and biofuels (CBG and ethanol blended fuels) - to address diverse customer needs while progressing towards decarbonisation, described as maximising carbon reduction potential, derisking and financial health.
- Strengthen the SUV portfolio while continuing to serve the small car and other passenger vehicle segments; plans to introduce 7 SUVs in the next 5 years.
- Treat India as a collection of numerous large and distinct markets and widen customer choice across vehicle segments, form factors and powertrain options within individual models, as the route to increasing market share.
- Grow exports as a pillar of future growth by leveraging Suzuki's global distribution network, including re-entering advanced markets such as Europe and Japan with e VITARA exports, under the 'Make in India, Make for the World' vision.
- Democratise safety as a product philosophy - six airbags and Electronic Stability Control offered as standard across nearly the entire domestic portfolio, with 5-star Bharat NCAP ratings on new models.
- Deepen non-urban and rural distribution, including scaling the compact NEXA Studio retail format, and expand sales, service and spare part outlets in line with faster rural growth.
- Continue digitalisation of the customer journey and of service operations (NEXAVERSE / ARENAVERSE, AI-powered virtual assistants, WhatsApp chatbot, Maruti Suzuki Smart Finance) to improve efficiency and customer convenience.
- Strengthen localisation, alternate sourcing and the supplier ecosystem as the core of supply chain resilience and of cost competitiveness in emerging technologies.
- Shift more outbound logistics to rail, supported by in-plant railway sidings at Manesar and planned at Kharkhoda, for cost saving, lower carbon load and lower transit damage.
- Work more closely and in a more integrated way with Suzuki Motor Corporation, Japan, to build new models in shorter and more cost-effective ways, while keeping transactions at arm's length.
- Pursue in-house biogas production as a clean, renewable, zero-import-content substitute for CNG, starting with four biogas plants in a first phase.
- Dividend policy is formal and published: the Company has formulated a dividend distribution policy available on its website, and for FY 2025-26 the Board recommended a dividend of INR 140 per equity share of INR 5 each, with no amount carried to General Reserve; the declaration is put to members as an ordinary resolution at the 45th AGM on 31st August 2026. The Chairman frames the payout as balancing shareholder return against reinvestment - 'This is consistent with the dividend policy and takes into account the massive investments being made by your company' - the investments being the accelerated capacity expansion (Kharkhoda, Hansalpur, the new Sanand site at a proposed INR 35,000 crores) and the first-phase biogas plants approved by the Board at INR 561 crores. The Company has a policy for determining material subsidiaries under Regulation 16(1)(c) of the Listing Regulations but had no material subsidiary as on 31st March 2026 following the amalgamation of Suzuki Motor Gujarat Private Limited into MSIL. During the year the Company neither invited nor accepted any deposits from the public; details of loans, guarantees and investments under Section 186 are stated to be in the notes to the financial statements, which were not routed here. No buyback, debt-reduction or credit-rating intent appears in the routed text.
- Occupational Health and Safety Management System aligned with ISO 45001:2018 implemented across all operational locations - manufacturing facilities, the R&D Centre, Head Office, zonal and regional offices, stockyards, port facilities, transit vehicle parks and Regional Parts Distribution Centres.
- ISO 45001:2018 certification held at the Gurugram and Manesar manufacturing facilities, the R&D Centre at Rohtak (Haryana) and the Head Office in New Delhi; the new greenfield facility at Kharkhoda and the recently amalgamated Hansalpur facility are in the process of obtaining certification - a dated, checkable open item.
- Zero fatalities among employees and workers in FY 2025-26 (also stated in the Chairman's message: 'The number of fatalities in accidents in our plants in FY 2025-26 were nil'); LTIFR of 0.007 for employees and 0.014 for workers per million person-hours.
- Safety governance supervised by the MD & CEO through a three-tier Plant / Division / Department Safety and Health Committee framework, Safety Ambassadors, HIRA with Work Instruction Sheets, an online work permit system with the KY (Kiken Yochi) hazard prediction process, independent third-party safety audits at all plant locations, and an Online Incident Reporting System deployed in March 2026.
- 100% of plants and offices (including Head Office) assessed for health and safety practices and for working conditions during the year.
- Decarbonisation target (Chairman's message): carbon footprint in the production process to reduce from the present 615,000 tonnes to 266,000 tonnes in FY 2030-31.
- Renewable electricity target (Chairman's message): to increase from the present 23% to 85% by FY 2030-31. The Board's Report energy-conservation annexure records the share rising from 21.3% to 22.8% during FY 2025-26, adding 35,767 MWh of renewable power (25,394 TCO2).
- Solar target (Chairman's message): solar energy use to rise from 79 MWp at end-FY 2025-26 to 319 MWp by 2030-31, of which 214 MWp generated in-house.
- Biogas: Board approval for four biogas plants in a first phase at a cost of INR 561 crores, with an intent to use over 20 tonnes of biogas per day by FY 2030-31, positioned as a zero-import-content substitute for CNG; work with the Indian Agricultural Research Institute, Pusa over the last two years supports the approach.
- Water: water intensity in the production process expected to decrease by 17% by FY 2030-31 versus FY 2025-26; Gurgaon and Manesar already awarded water positive certificates, with Kharkhoda and Hansalpur to follow.
- Multi-pathway decarbonisation strategy rather than a single technology - ICE, CNG, biofuels (CBG and ethanol blended fuels), hybrid and electric - stated to maximise carbon reduction potential, derisking and financial health; green vehicles (CNG, mild hybrid, strong hybrid, BEV) reached nearly 52% of total PV sales in FY 2025-26 versus about 48% in FY 2024-25.
- Product safety as an ESG commitment: six airbags and Electronic Stability Control standard on nearly 100% of the portfolio (the only OEM in the country to do so), 5-star Bharat NCAP ratings on VICTORIS and e VITARA, and full fleet compliance with Indian emission and safety regulations including CAFE Phase 2.
- Sustainable sourcing and supplier governance through Basic Purchase Agreements, Green Procurement Guidelines and a Supplier Code of Conduct, with 100% of Tier-1 suppliers stated to operate in line with these guidelines; 2,556 awareness programmes for value chain partners covering carbon neutrality, human rights, POSH, occupational health and safety, conflict minerals and cyber security, covering 100% of Tier-1 suppliers and dealers by value of business.
- Environment- and social-linked investment intensity disclosed in BRSR: 65.88% of R&D spend (FY 2024-25: 62.82%) and 54.66% of capex (FY 2024-25: 30.20%) directed at technologies improving environmental and social impacts, including the dedicated EV manufacturing facility at Hansalpur, new powertrains, in-plant railway sidings at Manesar, renewable energy capacity and storage, and rainwater harvesting infrastructure.
- Downstream network decarbonisation: workshop paint operations migrated from solvent-based to water-based paints, more than 300 dealer workshops on rooftop solar of nearly 22 MWp combined, and 1,067 kWp of rooftop solar commissioned at the Bengaluru and Nagpur Regional Parts Distribution Centres.
- Anti-bribery and anti-corruption framework - Code of Business Conduct and Ethics, Corporate Gifting Policy, Code of Business Conduct for Senior Management and a Supplier Code of Conduct extending expectations to Tier-1 suppliers - with nil disciplinary actions on bribery/corruption charges against Directors, KMPs, employees or workers and nil conflict-of-interest complaints in FY 2025-26 and FY 2024-25.
- BRSR reported on a standalone basis for FY 2025-26 and externally assured by Bureau Veritas (India) Private Limited - reasonable assurance on BRSR Core KPIs and limited assurance on other BRSR indicators; FY 2024-25 comparatives restated for the SMG amalgamation.
- CSR: two percent of average net profit under Section 135 was INR 2,454.21 million against a total amount spent for the financial year of INR 2,404.58 million plus INR 185.85 million brought-forward excess set off, leaving INR 136.22 million available for set-off in succeeding years; nil unspent CSR for the preceding three financial years. CSR is concentrated in community development, skill development (Japan India Institute of Manufacturing and ITI upgradation) and road safety (Automated Driving Test Tracks, IDTRs, Road Safety Knowledge Centres), independently impact-assessed by EY.
outlook.title: Strategy & capital allocation

outlook.body: MD&A: 'Considering India's long-term growth potential and the expanding export opportunity, the Company has laid out a capacity expansion roadmap to scale production capacity to four million units per annum over the next few years.' During FY 2025-26 production ramp-up at the greenfield Kharkhoda (Haryana) facility progressed steadily, and in FY 2026-27 the Company will commission two new manufacturing plants of 250,000 units annual capacity each - one at Kharkhoda, Haryana and the other at Hansalpur, Gujarat. Planning for subsequent expansion phases continued in parallel, and all new manufacturing facilities are being designed with multi-powertrain flexibility so they can respond to future shifts in technology and customer demand; the Chairman adds that new production lines are being made flexible enough to change platforms and models as required. The Chairman's message gives the project-level detail: two lines have been commissioned at Kharkhoda with work progressing on the third; a fourth line of 250,000 capacity was commissioned at Hansalpur, 'raising installed capacity to 1 million. This is Suzuki's largest plant anywhere in the world'; work has started at a new site in Sanand, Gujarat where a total capacity of 1 million units is intended, with a proposed investment of INR 35,000 crores; and as a result of these expansion projects installed capacity 'would reach 2.9 million units at the end of FY 2026-27 and 3.65 million units at the end of FY 2030-31'. The MD&A also records that the amalgamation of Suzuki Motor Gujarat Private Limited was completed (effective 1 December 2025, appointed date 1 April 2025) and that an additional greenfield manufacturing facility in Gujarat has been announced. Beyond vehicle assembly, the BRSR lists where environment- and social-linked capex went - 'Construction of dedicated EV manufacturing facility at Hansalpur', investments in new powertrains, in-plant railway sidings at Manesar, expansion of installed renewable energy capacity and storage, digital initiatives for process optimisation and energy efficiency, infrastructure for increasing the use of renewable electricity, product safety and quality, business continuity and rainwater harvesting infrastructure - and states that 54.66% of total capex in FY 2025-26 went to such technologies versus 30.20% in FY 2024-25 (R&D: 65.88% versus 62.82%). The Chairman flags a railway siding planned at Kharkhoda on the pattern of the working Manesar siding, and Board approval to start four biogas plants in a first phase at a cost of INR 561 crores. Network build-out ran alongside plant capex: 366 sales outlets added in FY 2025-26 (868 new sales and service touchpoints taking the total to 10,527 per the Chairman), the NEXA Studio compact format scaled up, service touchpoints at 5,926, the parts distributor network expanded by a record 197 outlets to 1,574 with 51 distributor warehouses added (the highest addition in a single year), own warehouse capacity and logistics hubs significantly expanded, more than 1,500 workshops equipped for EV service, more than 300 dealer workshops on rooftop solar totalling nearly 22 MWp, and rooftop solar of 1,067 kWp commissioned at the Bengaluru and Nagpur Regional Parts Distribution Centres.

outlook.body:
- GST reform of 22 September 2025 was the key inflection point: it improved affordability and revived small car demand, turning a 0.4% y-o-y industry decline in H1 FY 2025-26 into 16.7% growth in H2; the Company's own domestic volumes swung from -5.6% in H1 to +12.3% in H2.
- Management expects that with affordability improving after GST reform, passenger vehicle demand is likely to realign more closely with India's economic growth trajectory, reversing the weakening of that relationship caused by entry-level affordability challenges.
- India remains one of the most under-penetrated passenger vehicle markets globally, with long-term growth potential driven by rising incomes and increasing aspirations for personal mobility.
- Growth in FY 2025-26 was constrained by production capacity rather than demand - the Company operated at nearly full capacity utilisation in H2 and ended the year with a large pending order book, which prompted acceleration of capacity expansion.
- Added capacity is the near-term volume driver: 500,000 units of manufacturing capacity added in FY 2026-27, which management says will take time to ramp up fully but is expected to enable volume growth of around 10% in FY 2026-27.
- First-time buyer participation rose to nearly 50% in H2 from about 42% in H1, with a large number of two-wheeler upgraders visiting showrooms - evidence of the entry-level segment reopening.
- Mix: SUVs continued to account for over 56% of industry PV sales, and MSIL's own SUV contribution rose to 31% in H2 from 26% in H1 after the VICTORIS and e VITARA launches.
- Powertrain mix shift towards cleaner technologies - CNG, SHEV and BEV rose to 28.9% of total industry PV sales from 24.4%; MSIL's green vehicle share reached nearly 52% of its PV sales versus about 48%.
- Margin driver: operating margin (as a % of net sales) moderated to 8.4% from 10.0%, driven by adverse commodity prices and supply-side pressures from geopolitical developments, with the Company refraining from passing on the full cost increases in order to support demand recovery.
- Near-term watch item: geopolitical tensions in West Asia may exert pressure on profitability through higher commodity prices, and risks related to availability of specialised materials and critical components are likely to persist.
- Exports are expected to be sustained at FY 2025-26 levels despite geopolitical uncertainty, supported by a diversified footprint spanning nearly 120 countries that provides resilience against country-specific disruptions.
- Non-urban demand: rural markets performed well through the year and urban markets recovered post GST reform; non-urban markets now contribute over 52% of sales versus about 48% previously.
- Chairman's market view: the car industry is estimated to grow to 6.1 to 6.3 million units by FY 2030-31, with the small car market share growing significantly faster than in the last five years, which could lead to changes in the Company's longer-term targets.
- At the end of FY 2025-26 the Company had around 190,000 pending customer orders, of which nearly 130,000 were in the small car segment, highlighting the strength of underlying demand.
- Chairman's message: 'We ended March with 1.9 lakh pending bookings, a result of inadequate manufacturing capacity of the models in demand.'
- Dealer inventory remained low at around 12 days of stock, reflecting continued strong retail demand since the GST reform.

risks.note: The Company aims to scale production to four million units annually by FY 2030-31, nearly double its current capacity. It took almost 40 years to reach two million units; the next two million is to be added in just 7-8 years, a pace nearly five times faster. This requires significantly more human capital, financial investment and technical know-how plus faster decision-making, and stakeholder partners - suppliers, dealers and transporters - must scale in tandem.
risks.risk: Risks associated with the increased scale of operations

risks.note: With nearly 450 Tier-1 and about 1,500 Tier-2 suppliers, supply disruption remains a major business continuity risk. Export restrictions on certain critical materials during the year highlighted the vulnerability of globally concentrated supply chains, and geopolitical tensions, trade restrictions and logistics disruptions may continue to affect supply availability. Mitigation is localisation, alternate sources, diversified sourcing locations and the Vendor Comprehensive Excellence Programme.
risks.risk: Continuity of component supplies across a concentrated supplier base

risks.note: Increasing adoption of advanced automotive technologies raises dependence on specialised materials and critical components whose supply chains remain concentrated in a few countries; in an increasingly dynamic geopolitical environment, material-availability risk is likely to persist. In the near term, geopolitical tensions in West Asia may exert pressure on profitability through higher commodity prices.
risks.risk: Dependence on specialised materials and critical components sourced from a limited number of countries

risks.note: Electrification, software-defined vehicles, advanced electronics and connectivity are transforming the industry, but several of these technologies are yet to reach the cost competitiveness needed for widespread adoption in a price-sensitive market such as India. As the BEV, SHEV and advanced-feature portfolio expands, holding cost competitiveness while preserving affordability is a key strategic priority, addressed through localisation, value engineering and supplier base expansion.
risks.risk: Cost competitiveness of emerging and advanced technologies in a price-sensitive market

risks.note: Sudden and significant increases in the prices of metals, energy and other commodities can adversely impact profitability and business performance, a risk reinforced by recent geopolitical developments. This risk materialised in FY 2025-26: operating margin moderated to 8.4% from 10.0%, driven by adverse commodity prices and supply-side pressures, with the Company choosing not to pass on the full cost increases. Mitigation includes consumption optimisation, alternate materials, material circularity, hedging, forward contracts and long-term commercial arrangements.

Scaling operations amid rapid technological transformation increases demand for new skillsets both internally and across value chain partners; at the same time, sustaining the organisational values, culture of partnership and continuous-improvement spirit built over four decades becomes harder as scale and workforce expand.
risks.risk: Capacity and capability for future readiness - skills, leadership pipeline and cultural continuity at scale

risks.note: Cyber threats are growing and the Company protects information assets through employee education on phishing and proactive monitoring. It has created a cybersecurity assessment framework based on global standards for suppliers, and over 400 Tier-1 supplier partners have been assessed so far, on the view that supply-chain cyber resilience is a business-continuity issue.
risks.risk: Cybersecurity, including cyber risk in the supply chain

risks.note: The Company is exposed to fluctuations in foreign exchange rates, mainly on the import of components, raw materials and services and on the export of vehicles and services. It runs a structured exchange risk management policy and uses hedge instruments judiciously depending on market conditions and the currency view. The MD&A separately records a sharp depreciation of the rupee against the US dollar towards the end of the year.
risks.risk: Foreign exchange exposure on imports and exports
